newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian election campaign opens without trouble.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian election campaign opens without trouble.

text.p: Indonesian political leaders spread out through the sprawling archipelago on Sunday at the start of a month-long general election campaign to woo nearly 125 million voters in the world's fourth-largest nation.

President Suharto's eldest daughter, businesswoman Siti Hardyanti "Tutut" Rukmana, joined other leaders in appealing for peace and unity when she kicked off the campaign of the ruling Golkar at Semarang in volatile central Java.
"We must be watchful of security. We must be orderly," she told about 10,000 people in the industrial port city. Tutut is also one of seven chairmen of Golkar.
Populous central Java has been hit by pre-campaign violence in recent weeks, primarily between supporters of Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP).

Golkar, the PPP and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), the only three groups legally permitted to contest the May 29 local and national elections, have agreed to campaign each day in separate areas of the country.

On Sunday, Golkar was campaigning across Java and in the remote Mulukus and Irian Jaya in the east. It is seeking more than 70 percent of the vote after taking 68 percent in the last elections in 1992.
The United Development Party, which won 17 percent of the vote in 1992, was campaigning in Sumatra, the resort island of Bali and its adjacent Nusa Tenggara islands.

The PDI, badly split since its leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted by government-backed rebels last year, was seeking voter backing in Kalimantan on Borneo island and Sulawesi. It took 15 percent in 1992.

Reuter correspondent Jim Della-Giacoma reported from Semarang that about 10,000 people were at the fairground, where Tutut also called on the electorate not to spoil their ballots or boycott the polls.
"We must all join in the general election because it ensures the future of the nation. You must not join 'golput' (spoil ballots or abstain from voting)," Tutut added.
A huge banner draped around a Ferris wheel on one side of the fairground proclaiming "Golkar is my choice" was ripped away by a stiff breeze during the rally.
Central Java was awash with yellow banners, vastly outnumbering the green symbol of the United Development Party and the red of the PDI.

Security was low-key with few troops in evidence. Golkar officials were providing the main security at the Semarang rally. Armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung has pledged the military would prevent violence.
Indonesian markets were jittery last week on fears of possible campaign violence. The rupiah dropped 20 points to 2,440.50 to the dollar before moving back to 2,436 by Saturday.
The Jakarta Stock Exchange was little changed on Friday, with the composite index closing at 652.4 points, but brokers attributed some profit-taking to election nerves.

"The crucial point is Sunday and Monday. People are looking at the start of the campaign which should give indications whether the authorities have things under control," a foreign exchange dealer said.
